segments.say: The boat comes to rest against a low wooden jetty, so gently that you hardly feel it. You step out, and your feet find soft, fresh snow. Just beyond the water, a small village lies sleeping on a gentle slope, its roofs covered in white. The snow is falling slowly, in large, soft flakes, and the whole world is hushed, as if someone has turned the volume of the night all the way down.

You walk slowly up a narrow lane between the houses. Every step makes a small, soft crunch, and then the snow swallows the sound. There's no traffic, no voices, no hurry. Only the quiet falling of the flakes, settling on the fences, on the window ledges, on the shoulders of your warm coat. Breathe in the cold, clean air. Breathe out, and watch your breath drift away like a little cloud.

In a few of the houses, a small lamp has been left on, glowing softly behind frosted glass. Everyone inside is asleep, tucked in under heavy blankets, warm and safe. The village is resting, all of it at once, and you're walking through it like a quiet guest who doesn't need to knock on any door. You belong here, just for tonight, in all this stillness.

Snow covers every footprint, sooner or later. Look behind you, and you'll see your own steps in the lane, already softening at the edges as the new flakes settle into them. By morning they'll be gone, smoothed over, as if no one had walked here at all. The small missteps of our lives are a lot like that. Time keeps falling on them, quietly, until they're hard to find.

show.text: Snow covers every footprint, sooner or later.

segments.say: At the top of the lane there's a small square, with a stone well in the middle wearing a round white cap of snow. From here you can see the whole village below you, every roof soft and white, every chimney breathing a thin line of smoke into the dark. The snow keeps falling, slowly, slowly, and the lamps glow gold in the blue night.

Under the wide eaves of an old house, there's a wooden bench, sheltered and dry, with a thick wool blanket folded on it. You sit down, wrap the blanket around you, and lean back against the wall. The snow falls just in front of you, a soft white curtain moving gently in the lamplight. Now we'll let the body rest, one part at a time.

Start with your toes. Notice them, tucked inside warm socks. Let them soften. Let them grow heavy and warm, as if they were sinking slowly into deep, soft snow that isn't cold at all. Breathe in. And as you breathe out, let that warmth spread into the soles of your feet, and into your heels, and up around your ankles.

Now your calves. Let them loosen, the way snow settles after it falls. Then your knees, soft and easy. Then your thighs, heavy and relaxed, resting on the bench, held by the blanket. There's nothing your legs need to do now. No more walking tonight. Breathe in slowly, and as you breathe out, let them sink a little more.

We're moving slowly upward, like snow drifting in reverse. Feet and legs, already heavy. Now the hips and belly. Then the back and shoulders. Then the arms and hands. Let your belly rise softly as you breathe in, and fall as you breathe out. Let your hips settle. Feel the whole lower half of your body resting, quiet and warm.

Now your back. Feel each part of it resting against the wall, one by one, from the bottom to the top. And your shoulders. They've carried a lot today, perhaps more than you noticed. Let them drop, just a little. Then a little more. Imagine soft snowflakes landing on them and melting away, taking the last of the tension with them.

Let the heaviness flow down your arms, from your shoulders to your elbows, from your elbows to your wrists. Your hands rest open in your lap, under the blanket, warm and loose. Your fingers uncurl. There's nothing to hold, nothing to carry, nothing to grip. Breathe in, slow and gentle. Breathe out, and feel your arms grow heavier still.

A face that's been held tight all day can finally rest. So now, your neck. Let it soften. Your jaw, loose, the teeth slightly apart. Your cheeks, the place that grew warm when an old memory came back, now cool and calm in the snowy air. Your eyes, heavy behind their lids. And your forehead, smooth and wide and still.

show.text: A face that's been held tight all day can finally rest.

segments.say: And last of all, the very top of your head. Imagine a few soft snowflakes landing there, light as breath, and melting slowly, sending a gentle coolness down over your scalp, your temples, the back of your neck. Every small muscle there can let go now. There's no thinking that needs to be done tonight. Only resting.

Softness spreads, the way snow does. One flake lands, then another, then a thousand, until the whole village is white and quiet. Relaxation works the same way. One part of the body lets go, and then the next, and the next, until the whole of you is resting under a soft, warm covering of calm. Breathe in. And breathe out.

show.text: Softness spreads, the way snow does.

segments.say: Somewhere, Ivy is lying just like this, soft from her toes to her forehead. She doesn't remember the moment she stopped thinking about the lecture hall. It simply drifted out of her mind, the way a snowflake lands and melts. Her breathing is slow and even now, and the room around her is warm and quiet.

Now feel your whole body at once, from your toes to the top of your head, heavy and warm and resting, like the village below, wrapped in its soft white blanket. Breathe in, and let the cool air fill you. Breathe out, and let your body sink just a little deeper. You are safe, and you are resting, and there's nothing left to do.

At the far edge of the village, a little apart from the other houses, you notice a small cottage with a warm orange glow in its window. Smoke rises from its chimney in a slow, steady line. The door is painted a deep, friendly red. And as you look at it, you have the quiet feeling that someone has kept the fire going, just for you.
